findings.detail: Core fund balances declining significantly from £48.995m (2024/25) to £25.361m (2028/29). This 48% reduction constrains financial flexibility, reduces capacity to self-fund capital or absorb shocks, and increases reliance on external borrowing to fund the capital programme.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial resilience and indicate increasing dependence on borrowing, heightening refinancing risk and limiting the council's options to respond to adverse conditions.
findings.figures: Fund balances £48.995m (2024/25 Actual) declining to £25.361m (2028/29 Estimate)

findings.paper_title: Item 5a - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 51% to £191.6m by 2028/29, driven by HRA borrowing plans up to £61.3m
findings.detail: Total CFR projected to grow from £126.6m (actual 2024/25) to £191.6m (2028/29), with HRA driving most growth (£104.7m to £166.0m, a 58% increase). HRA capital plans include up to £61.3m of new borrowing to 2028/29, some contingent on property acquisitions. This represents a significant structural increase in the council's underlying borrowing need and future debt service obligations.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing capital financing requirements signal substantial future debt service costs and revenue pressure, directly affecting the council's financial sustainability and key debt metrics that lenders monitor.
findings.figures: CFR £126.622m (2024/25 actual) to £191.568m (2028/29); HRA CFR £104.736m to £166.044m; HRA planned borrowing £61.308m
findings.quote: HRA capital plans now include borrowing totalling up to £61.308m up to 2028/29. Some of this is opportunity led acquisitions and so will only be drawn down if land or property acquisitions are identified.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: CFO expresses unprecedented concern about settlement timing and sustainability; no considered financial plan possible due to two-day notice of major changes
findings.detail: The S151 Officer's statutory statement (Section 7) is unusual in tone. She explicitly states: 'It is disappointing that there has been significant and unprecedented change in funding between the Provisional Settlement and Final Settlement...the very late notice of the change (two days before the publication of this report) means that considered plans to offset the impact, including with Member consultation, have not been possible.' She concludes that 'the medium-term position is more challenging' and requires 'continued focus on sound financial management and governance as part of this process'—language indicating material concern.
findings.matters: The S151 Officer's formal assessment is a material governance signal. Her explicit statement that 'considered plans' were not possible indicates the council is operating with incomplete financial strategy for the medium term.
findings.figures: Budget approval timeline: final settlement 9 February 2026, papers published 11 February 2026
findings.quote: It is disappointing that there has been significant and unprecedented change in funding between the Provisional Settlement and Final Settlement. Although an offsetting grant for one year is appreciated, the very late notice of the change (two days before the publication of this report) means that considered plans to offset the impact, including with Member consultation, have not been possible.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation vesting date 1 April 2028 creates £3.5m+ reserve commitment and operational planning uncertainty
findings.detail: All councils in Gloucestershire are planning to cease operations on 31 March 2028, replaced by one or two successor councils. Stroud has set aside £2m for its share of the LGR transition costs and a further £1.5m for internal costs (staff secondment backfill, recruitment and retention support, training). The S151 Officer notes there is 'no forewarning' of LGR timing changes from central government, and if the date slips, the council will need additional work to pass a sustainable position to a successor.
findings.matters: LGR creates a hard deadline for financial planning but also uncertainty: successor council structures and boundaries are not yet finalised, and costs and timing may change. A council borrowing in this context faces uncertainty about asset ownership post-vesting.
findings.figures: £2m LGR transition funding (council share); £1.5m LGR-related costs; planned vesting date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: It is currently expected that the council, along with all councils in Gloucestershire, ceasing to exist on 1 April 2028, with one or two successor councils vesting on the same day.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Loss of £140k per annum waste incentive grant from Gloucestershire County Council starting 2027/28
findings.detail: Gloucestershire County Council has signalled it will withdraw £140k annual waste incentives to district councils from 2027/28. This is a firm future reduction built into a year already facing the £1.026m settlement reduction.
findings.matters: Multi-agency funding dependencies create timing risk. A combined £1.166m pressure in 2027/28 (£1.026m settlement + £140k waste incentive) with no identified mitigation is material.
findings.figures: £140k pa waste incentive withdrawal from 2027/28
findings.quote: the expected removal of waste incentives from Gloucestershire County Council (£140k pa) from 2027/28

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) waste income uncertain and expected to decline; actual allocation may fall below budgeted £1.3m
findings.detail: The council is budgeting £1.3m for EPR income in 2026/27, but the actual allocation is contingent on producers' fee collection and is expected to reduce over time as businesses limit packaging waste to avoid EPR costs. The 2025/26 initial allocation was £1.413m but uplifted to £1.579m; however, 'these allocations are dependent on the collection of fees from packaging producers and so are not guaranteed'.
findings.matters: EPR is a new, unproven income stream that directly incentivises businesses to reduce waste entering the system. Budget volatility and downside risk are material, and the council has already assumed conservatively at £1.3m.
findings.figures: EPR budget 2026/27: £1.3m (vs initial allocation estimate £1.579m); actual 2025/26 revised up to £1.579m from £1.413m
findings.quote: The anticipated allocation for 2026/27 is £1.615m, but these allocations are dependent on the collection of fees from packaging producers and so are not guaranteed. The MTFP currently includes £1.300m for 2026/27 to reflect a potential lower collection from producers and therefore payment from government, and reducing income levels over the medium term as businesses seek to limit EPR costs through changed behaviour.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Investment income halved by interest rate falls: £485k reduction in 2026/27 and further £236k in 2027/28
findings.detail: Bank of England rate cuts from 4.5% in April 2025 to 3.75% in December 2025 have shrunk investment returns. The council's target investment income is falling £485k in 2026/27 alone. This reflects both lower rates and declining reserves available to invest, indicating the council is drawing down balances to manage current spending.
findings.matters: Investment income loss is a leading indicator of reserve depletion. A council losing £721k of investment income over two years is either holding less cash or deploying it to operations rather than keeping it liquid.
findings.figures: Investment income reduction: £485k in 2026/27; further £236k reduction in 2027/28
findings.quote: The target investment income is reduced by £485k in 2026/27 and a further £236k in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Council tax base growth assumption cut from 1.5% to 1.02%, and second homes council tax premium down 27% (525 to 381 properties)
findings.detail: The final settlement confirmed lower council tax base growth than the provisional MTFP assumed, reducing expected income by approximately £58k pa. The second homes premium—a revenue source that should correlate to planning and housing demand—fell from 525 to 381 properties, a 27% decline. The council attributes this to residents properly registering circumstances after the premium was introduced, but it signals either lower second home ownership or better compliance behaviour.
findings.matters: Council tax is the largest revenue source, and growth assumptions underpin medium-term plans. A falling second homes premium may indicate demand weakness or property market softening in the district.
findings.figures: Council tax base growth: 1.02% (vs 1.5% assumption); £58k annual income reduction; second homes paying premium: 381 (down from 525)
findings.quote: Growth in the tax base has been confirmed at 1.02%, which is lower than the 1.5% assumed within the MTFP reported in the Budget Strategy. This will mean a reduction in council tax funding of approximately £58k pa.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Business rates income reset removes existing growth and eliminates the business rates pool gain of unknown value
findings.detail: As part of the Fair Funding Review, business rates growth accumulated since the 2013 reset will be removed and baseline income will revert to £2.6m. The Gloucestershire business rates pool, which generated a gain used in baseline funding calculations, will cease to exist from April 2026. The document does not specify the size of the pool gain being lost, but notes its removal has reduced the funding protection available.
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile and subject to revaluation, appeals, and economic conditions. Losing accumulated growth creates downside risk if actual collections fall below the £2.6m floor. The council's CFO notes 'there is added risk of being below baseline levels'.
findings.figures: Baseline business rates £2.6m; Business Rates protection 100% in 2026/27, reducing to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29
findings.quote: the reset of business rates growth has a significant impact on the levels of business rates retained by the council, as set out in Funding Table, Table 1 following para 2.16...existing growth in the system will be removed and retained income will drop back down to baseline levels of £2.6m.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account position has worsened; £13m additional borrowing needed for major works with costs payable from rental income
findings.detail: The HRA faces increased compliance costs for damp and mould, electrical testing, and other regulatory burdens described as 'an unaffordable position without additional borrowing'. The council is borrowing £13m for HRA major works beyond the baseline capital programme, and these borrowing costs will need to be paid from rental income from existing homes rather than from capital receipts or grants. This creates a direct burden on tenant rents or reserves.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing is backed by rental income. Additional debt serviced from existing rental streams reduces financial headroom and constrains the ability to invest in new affordable housing or absorb void losses.
findings.figures: £13m borrowing for HRA major works; total HRA capital programme £38.976m in 2026/27 rising to £49.686m total with HRA
findings.quote: Due to the position set out in the HRA budget setting papers there is also borrowing of £13m for Major Works. The borrowing costs will need to be paid from rental income from existing homes.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: Savings of at least £571k have been introduced but not allocated to any service or activity
findings.detail: The council has inserted unallocated savings targets into the MTFP following the funding shock, but has not decided what services to cut or reduce. An additional £83k saving identified in 2024/25 was not realised and now sits as a target. The council states it will determine where these cuts fall during a review process concurrent with the next budget round beginning summer 2026, meaning the current budget approval includes placeholders with no operational plan.
findings.matters: Unknown savings targets indicate the council's spending plans are not yet grounded in operational reality. Lenders need to know whether pledged service levels or capital programmes will have to be cut.
findings.figures: £571k total savings target (£488k ongoing plus £83k unachieved from 2024/25)
findings.quote: These savings are not currently allocated to specific services or activities and will be subject to a separate decision.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget 2026-27 Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Plan
findings.headline: £1.026m annual funding reduction from 2027/28 and a £5.1m structural deficit from 2030/31 when transitional support ends
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review introduces a major funding reset. The provisional settlement promised transitional protection at 95% of current levels, but the final settlement announced on 9 February 2026 (two days before this budget was published) removed £734k in 2026/27, offset by a one-off grant. From 2027/28, £1.026m annual reductions are embedded into the MTFP, representing 4.5% of funding available. Beyond the three-year settlement in 2030/31, the deficit is forecast at £5.1m when protections cease.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can service debt from a sustainable revenue base. These reductions are structural, not cyclical, and have no identified solution.
findings.figures: £1.026m annual reduction 2027/28–2028/29; £5.1m deficit in 2030/31; transitional protection reduces to 95% from 2026/27
findings.quote: The Final Settlement shows a much bigger change than would ordinarily be expected following the Provisional Settlement being announced, and although top up funding has been included to ensure that 2026/27 financial year is not impacted, a reduction in funding of £1.026m in the years 2027/28 and 2028/29 is now expected.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: New homes programme requires £1.94m to £2.37m government subsidy per project; James Sleeman Close alone needs £1.94m-£2.37m to be affordable
findings.detail: The council is requesting capital budget for two new build schemes: James Sleeman Close (9 houses, £3.009m total) and May Lane (17 dwellings, £6.040m total). For James Sleeman Close, 'At full affordable rents (80% of market value), subsidy of £1.94m would be needed. If social rents are to be charged subsidy of £2.37m would be required.' The council is hoping to access Homes England Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) 2026-2036, expected to open for bidding from February 2026. Schemes cannot proceed without identifying subsidy.
findings.matters: Capital ambition is hostage to securing government grant funding. Bidding risk is real (competition, changing priorities). If bids fail, these schemes cannot proceed without unsustainable HRA borrowing. New builds will add operational costs (maintenance, management) immediately but generate rental income only over decades.
findings.figures: James Sleeman Close: £3.009m total, requires £1.94m-£2.37m subsidy; May Lane: £6.040m total; SAHP bidding expected February 2026
findings.quote: At full affordable rents (80% of market value), subsidy of £1.94m would be needed. If social rents are to be charged subsidy of £2.37m would be required in order to ensure no impact to the HRA revenue position over 45 years.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: Awaab's Law (damp/mould compliance) commenced 27 October 2025 with strict statutory timelines; council has set £1.065m capital budget and hired compliance team
findings.detail: Phase 1 of Awaab's Law commenced 27 October 2025 and requires the council to investigate and resolve damp/mould hazards to strict statutory timelines. The council has already purchased equipment and appointed 'a small internal damp and mould team consisting of administrators, surveyors and a multiskilled operative.' It is requesting £1.065m capital budget based on 426 referrals last year at estimated £2,500 per case. Phase 2 is expected in 2026 covering additional HHSRS hazards.
findings.matters: This is an active, unfunded mandate with hard deadlines and significant financial impact. Non-compliance carries regulatory enforcement risk and potential enforcement notices. Demand is escalating (referral-driven) and future phases are not yet known, making forecasting difficult.
findings.figures: 426 referrals last year; £2,500 average cost per case; £1.065m capital budget for 2026/27; Phase 1 commenced 27 October 2025
findings.quote: Phase 1 of Awaab's Law commenced on 27 October 2025 and introduces strict timelines for addressing damp and mould hazards. Additional equipment has been purchased and a small internal damp and mould team consisting of administrators, surveyors and a multiskilled operative have been appointed to ensure compliance with phase 1 of Awaab's law.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: Current asset management IT systems are inadequate and pose 'high risk to operational delivery, regulatory compliance, financial forecasting, and long-term asset sustainability'
findings.detail: The council states: 'Our systems are not suitable and are inadequate for asset management functions...This represents a high risk to operational delivery, regulatory compliance, financial forecasting, and long-term asset sustainability.' It is requesting £350k capital to replace the system, with implementation costs (staff backfill, consultant support) in the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Poor asset data quality undermines financial forecasting, compliance evidence, and investment planning. This is a control weakness that compounds uncertainty about capital costs and asset condition. For a lender, inadequate systems increase the risk that reported costs are understated.
findings.figures: £350k capital budget for new Asset Management System
findings.quote: Our systems are not suitable and are inadequate for asset management functions, particularly due to limitations within its compliance capabilities. This represents a high risk to operational delivery, regulatory compliance, financial forecasting, and long-term asset sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: Medium-term financial position has worsened from February 2025 MTFP due to additional legislative requirements and newly identified capital costs
findings.detail: The council's own statement: 'The medium term position of the HRA has worsened from the last MTFP in February 2025, largely due to additional legislative requirements and newly identified capital costs.' The MTFP table (Table 3) shows general reserves declining, and the council plans a comprehensive housing service review in 2026/27 (not expected to drive savings, only 'better align the service').
findings.matters: This signals deteriorating financial trajectory rather than stabilisation. The need for an unbudgeted service review suggests the council is not confident its current cost base is sustainable. Lenders track trend direction and confidence signalling.
findings.figures: MTFP worsened since February 2025; reserves declining per Table 3 and Graph 2
findings.quote: The medium term position of the HRA has worsened from the last MTFP in February 2025, largely due to additional legislative requirements and newly identified capital costs, as set out in the Housing Context section.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: Rent convergence has been delayed to April 2027 (not April 2026), continuing £1.19m annual income loss for another year
findings.detail: Currently only 14.3% of Stroud's social rent tenants pay formula rent; 85.7% pay below it, costing the HRA approximately £1.19m per year in lost income. The government's January 2026 policy paper confirmed rent convergence will begin April 2027 (with additional £1/week) then April 2028 (additional £2/week), 12 months later than previously hoped. The council notes it is 'disappointed that this has not been introduced from 1 April 2026' but describes convergence as 'welcome' because it provides funds to meet regulatory requirements.
findings.matters: Income loss persists through 2026/27, adding to borrowing pressure. The delay pushes the point at which the council can reinvest rental income back another year. A lender tracking HRA cash position needs this timing.
findings.figures: £1.19m annual income loss; 85.7% of tenants below formula rent; convergence now April 2027 (£1/week) then April 2028 (£2/week)
findings.quote: Currently only 14.3% of tenants have rents equivalent to the formula rent, with 85.7% with rents lower than formula rent. The average social rent is £6.03 per week lower than formula rent. This equates to reduced income of approximately £1.19m per year which is a significant financial pressure for the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: Multiple new regulatory requirements (Awaab's Law, electrical safety, fire safety, Consumer Standards) have no government funding but are driving £1.19m annual capital cost escalation
findings.detail: The paper states 'The social housing sector has experienced the greatest reshape in recent history' with new requirements in fire safety, electrical safety (5-year cycle from May 2026), damp/mould (Awaab's Law), Consumer Standards compliance, and a new Decent Homes Standard coming in 2035. Each imposes statutory deadlines and compliance obligations. Critically, 'there has been no additional new burdens funding to deliver any of the new requirements.' Major voids budget alone increases £283k due to rising costs for 'fabric repairs, structural works, damp and mould remediation, ventilation upgrades, roofing, and essential heating and electrical compliance works.'
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory burdens drive capital spend and staffing costs with no corresponding revenue relief. Non-compliance carries enforcement risk and potential tenant safety liability. A lender needs to know whether the council is adequately resourced to meet these deadlines.
findings.figures: £1.19m annual rent loss due to below-formula rents; £283k major voids increase; £1.065m damp and mould dedicated budget; electrical compliance, fire safety, and Consumer Standards all unfunded
findings.quote: The social housing sector has experienced the greatest reshape in recent history and there are now several new regulatory expectations that social landlords must meet. Whilst there is a known rent settlement in place, there has been no additional new burdens funding to deliver any of the new requirements.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Revised 202526 And Original 202627 and Housing Revenue Account MTFP
findings.headline: HRA requires £13m additional borrowing over the medium term because rent income cannot support capital works
findings.detail: The council states the HRA position is 'not supportable with existing rents, and additional borrowing is needed to support the Major Works capital programme.' This includes £7.5m in 2026/27, £2.5m in 2027/28 and £3.0m in 2028/29. The council already carries £111.743m borrowing (£97.717m external from PWLB). The paper notes this 'isn't just a short term problem and extends over an extended period.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand total borrowing exposure and whether the HRA's revenue position is deteriorating or stabilising. This signals the council is stretched to fund its housing stock maintenance and faces medium-term structural pressure.
findings.figures: £13m over medium term; £7.5m 2026/27, £2.5m 2027/28, £3.0m 2028/29; existing borrowing £111.743m (£97.717m external)
findings.quote: The increase costs mean that the position is not supportable with existing rents, and additional borrowing is needed to support the Major Works capital programme. As set out in section 10, this is a total of £13m over the medium term. It should be noted that this isn't just a short term problem and extends over an extended period.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £3.778m carried forward to 2025/26, with main delays in leisure centre, vehicles, and HRA projects
findings.detail: Capital expenditure underspent by £6.535m in 2024/25, with £3.778m of slippage approved to carry forward. Main items: Stratford Park & Lido maintenance £0.776m (delay during insourcing), multi-service contract vehicles £1.151m (manufacturer lead times), HRA capital £1.665m.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: General Fund strategy assumes Local Government Reorganisation on 1 April 2028; deficits planned through 2028/29 will be covered from General Fund Equalisation Reserve
findings.detail: The 2025/26 General Fund budget includes a £233k deficit funded from the General Fund Equalisation Reserve (£6.422m). The council plans to continue covering annual deficits from this reserve through 2028/29, explicitly stating this approach is reasonable only in anticipation of LGR proceeding on schedule.
findings.matters: The council's financial strategy depends entirely on LGR occurring as planned. If LGR is delayed or does not proceed, the council would face a structural deficit with limited reserves remaining to cover ongoing shortfalls, potentially requiring significant spending cuts or new borrowing.
findings.figures: £233k deficit in 2025/26; General Fund Equalisation Reserve £6.422m; deficits planned through 2028/29; anticipated LGR date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: In anticipation of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) on 1 April 2028, the Council considers it reasonable to utilise and reduce this reserve ahead of its anticipated integration into a new unitary authority. Officers have confirmed this understanding and are planning accordingly, while recognising that any changes to the LGR timeline would require a reassessment of the financial strategy to maintain balance.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Management has still not documented its review of pension fund valuations after three consecutive audit recommendations (2022/23 through 2024/25).
findings.detail: The council's external actuary (Hymans Robertson LLP) prepares pension valuations using assumptions including CPI, RPI and discount rates. Auditors have recommended management document their review and challenge of these assumptions for three years, but management has not changed their approach. While auditors were satisfied the assumptions were reasonable, management is not demonstrating its own expertise or challenge over a major balance sheet liability.
findings.matters: Pension fund liability is typically the largest liability on a council balance sheet; lack of documented challenge to actuarial assumptions by management suggests weak governance and indicates auditors, not management, are verifying the valuation accuracy.
findings.figures: Pension fund net liability value not specified but identified as significant risk in audit
findings.quote: Management have not changed their consideration of this recommendation, where there should be some consideration of the overall assumptions used by the valuer (e.g. salary increase estimate) compared to the internal expectations of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Employee payroll costs cannot be reconciled from underlying payroll records to the financial statements, a control weakness acknowledged but not yet resolved.
findings.detail: Testing of staff costs identified that the employee benefits expense line in the accounts cannot be reconciled back to payroll records. Management acknowledged this deficiency and committed to improve the reconciliation process and documentation for 2025/26, indicating this has been an ongoing issue.
findings.matters: Inability to reconcile payroll (a major operating expense) to source records represents a material control weakness over one of the council's largest spending lines and limits auditor assurance over expense accuracy.
findings.figures: Specific value not itemised but employee benefits is a material expense category
findings.quote: From our testing of staff costs, we were unable to reconcile the employee benefits expense line from the financial statements back to the payroll records.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditors identified £836k of known misstatements that management chose not to correct, including further PPE valuation errors.
findings.detail: During audit work, three categories of error were identified but management did not adjust them: investment interest income overstated by £195k, the council's share of pension fund asset overstatement of £108k, and PPE additions incorrectly included in carrying amounts for £533k. While each was individually below the materiality threshold of £1,872k, they accumulated to £836k in known but uncorrected errors.
findings.matters: Accumulated unadjusted errors in asset and pension valuations, particularly when combined with the prior period PPE error, suggest systemic control weaknesses in valuations that could mask the true financial position.
findings.figures: £836k total: £195k investment interest, £108k pension fund assets, £533k PPE
findings.quote: The table below provides details of adjustments identified during the 2024/25 audit which have not been made within the final set of financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Air source heat pump additions worth £5.5m were not properly accounted for in the 2023/24 valuations, requiring a material prior period restatement.
findings.detail: Audit work identified that three buildings had air source heat pump installations totalling £5,471k in 2023/24 that were not properly separated from the revalued asset values, despite the external valuer being aware of the additions. The prior year valuations for these buildings were materially overstated. Management have now restated the 2023/24 comparatives and adjusted 2024/25 entries accordingly, affecting multiple lines across the primary financial statements.
findings.matters: A £5.5m error in prior-year asset valuation indicates weakness in controls over capital additions and asset separation, raising questions about the accuracy of the council's asset base and whether other valuations might contain similar errors.
findings.figures: £5,471k in additions totalling £4,938k restated across 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.quote: On investigation we identified that the differences related to additions in 2023/24 for air source heat pumps installed at each of the buildings in 2023/24. The total value of these additions was £5,471k.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Community Services and Licensing Budget Monitoring Report Q2 202526
findings.headline: Leisure redevelopment requiring material borrowing decision coming to council in January 2026
findings.detail: Capital works on Active Lifestyles Stroud and the Lido have been deliberately held pending a strategic review. The council is preparing a business case that will detail the costs of a proposed redevelopment of the leisure centre, Lido and park, together with the borrowing required and expected return. This will be presented to council in January/February 2026.
findings.matters: Major capital borrowing decisions for strategic facilities are core credit metrics; the business case will determine debt implications and the council's capital strategy
findings.figures: Active Lifestyles and Lido capital budget £1.331m (revised), forecast spend £201k, variance (£1.171m)
findings.quote: A business case is being prepared to outline the indicative costs of the proposal, the amount of borrowing required and the return on the proposed investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Funds and Investment Risk Earmarked Reserve
findings.headline: Investment Risk Reserve will fall from £586k to £275k after absorbing 2025/26 losses, consuming 53% of remaining capacity
findings.detail: Reserve opens 1 April 2025 at £586k (itself depleted by the prior-year £907k Lothbury loss). The £311k losses will be charged to the reserve, reducing it to £275k. Council confirms no impact on general fund outturn, but the buffer for future investment volatility is substantially eroded.
findings.matters: While immediate general fund impact is contained, rapid reserve depletion limits the council's capacity to absorb further investment losses without affecting revenue finances
findings.figures: Opening balance £586k; estimated 2025/26 losses £311k; estimated closing balance £275k
findings.quote: This can be funded within the existing reserve and so there is no expectation of any impact on the general fund outturn position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Funds and Investment Risk Earmarked Reserve
findings.headline: Lothbury and Hermes property fund investments are crystallizing £311k in combined capital losses in 2025/26
findings.detail: Lothbury's £4m initial investment has fallen to £347k valuation, generating a £120k capital loss. Hermes' £2m investment has fallen to £1.8m, generating a £191k capital loss. Both funds are being liquidated due to investor redemptions and property market decline. This adds to a £907k loss crystallized from Lothbury in 2024/25.
findings.matters: Cumulative investment losses exceeding £1.2m signal deterioration in council's property fund strategy and exposure to market volatility
findings.figures: Lothbury: £4m initial → £347,033.30 valuation, £120k loss; Hermes: £2m initial → £1,823,147.81 valuation, £191k loss; prior-year Lothbury loss £907k
findings.quote: The total estimated loss set out in this report is £311k (£120k from Lothbury and £191k from Hermes).

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Auditors Annual Report - 2024_25 (November 2025)
findings.headline: Council unable to track whether £1.223m of planned 2024/25 savings were actually delivered
findings.detail: The council does not report on progress against budgeted savings targets during the year or in the outturn. While the year-end position shows the council met its overall budget, there is no evidence showing whether the specific £1.223m of identified savings were achieved or whether underspends came from elsewhere. This is an unresolved recommendation from the prior year audit.
findings.matters: If planned savings are not being tracked and achieved, future budget plans built on similar savings targets are unreliable and future deficits may be larger than forecast.
findings.figures: £1.223 million of identified savings in 2024/25; no dedicated reporting mechanism to track savings achievement
findings.quote: There is no evidence of specific reporting which tracks the savings targets set out at the start of the year to monitor their achievement throughout the year.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Auditors Annual Report - 2024_25 (November 2025)
findings.headline: General Fund deficit strategy depends on Local Government Reorganisation happening on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: The council's MTFP plans to fund General Fund deficits from the General Fund Equalisation Reserve through 2028/29, with deficits of £233k in 2025/26 continuing through the period. Officers acknowledge that if the LGR timeline changes, financial strategy will need reassessment.
findings.matters: If Local Government Reorganisation is delayed or does not proceed, the council will face budget gaps it has not planned to fill, creating medium-term financial uncertainty.
findings.figures: £233k deficit 2025/26; £6.422m General Fund Equalisation Reserve at start of 2025/26; deficits continue through 2028/29
findings.quote: In anticipation of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) on 1 April 2028, the Council considers it reasonable to utilise and reduce this reserve ahead of its anticipated integration into a new unitary authority.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Auditors Annual Report - 2024_25 (November 2025)
findings.headline: Housing stock survey gap creates unknown maintenance liability while HRA reserves are being depleted
findings.detail: Only 27-34% of council housing has been surveyed for condition in the last five years, against a target of over 90%. The auditors describe this as 'concerning' given that stock condition surveys determine HRA maintenance budgeting. With £5.19m being drawn from HRA reserves in 2025/26, any unexpected repairs could exceed budget.
findings.matters: Unknown maintenance liability creates financial risk while the HRA is drawing down reserves to a critical level. If repair costs prove higher than forecast, the council will lack reserves to cover them.
findings.figures: 27.5%-34.3% actual vs >90% target; £5.19m reserves drawn in 2025/26; reserves fall to £1.806m from £4.918m
findings.quote: If significant repairs and maintenance arise on the housing stock which has not been surveyed, this could give rise to large amounts of expenditure which have not been budgeted for in their entirety.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 2025/26 Action Plan
findings.headline: Stroudwater Canal capital project has secured £6.46m additional lottery grant but council lacks construction management expertise
findings.detail: National Lottery Heritage Fund has approved £6.46m additional grant for the canal project. The council acknowledges it has limited experience with construction management contracts and lacks technical expertise, having engaged a specialist external construction solicitor. Project governance arrangements remain under development with only 10% completion on contract management procedures.
findings.matters: Major capital project with significant external funding creates financial exposure; acknowledged expertise gaps and underdeveloped governance could increase delivery risk and impact project outcomes and the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £6.46m additional grant, 10% completion on procurement and contract management
findings.quote: The council has limited experience with construction management contracts and the proposed procurement route, and it currently lacks the technical expertise and capacity to support this aspect of the project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 2025/26 Action Plan
findings.headline: Stroud will vote on local government reorganisation on 20 November with joint submission to Government by 28 November
findings.detail: Stroud District Council is participating in a Gloucestershire-wide local government reorganisation process. Full Council will vote on unitary authority proposals on 20 November 2025, following which all councils will make a joint submission to Government by 28 November. An internal Programme Management Office is currently being scoped to support the wider programme, though resource arrangements remain at early stage (0% completion on ensuring adequate resources).
findings.matters: Organizational restructuring of this scale could affect the council's financial stability, borrowing capacity, management continuity, and service delivery during transition—material concerns for lenders assessing credit risk.
findings.figures: 20 November 2025, 28 November 2025, 0%
findings.quote: All proposals will be considered by Stroud District Council's Full Council on 20 November, with other councils reviewing the proposals through their respective decision-making processes ahead of a joint submission to Government by the 28 November.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Local plan non-compliance: escalated to Strategic Risk Register and will impact planning/development delivery
findings.detail: The risk relating to successful delivery of an up-to-date local plan has been escalated to the Strategic Risk Register at the request of the Senior Leadership Team. Non-compliance with national legislation is rated High Risk (score 9, Likely/Major). The risk will be monitored and updated as changes occur.
findings.matters: An outdated or non-compliant local plan constrains the council's ability to approve development, deliver capital schemes, and generate planning income, and exposes the council to intervention from the Planning Inspectorate.
findings.figures: Risk score 9 (Likely/Major); escalated to SLT at request
findings.quote: This risk relating to the successful delivery of a local plan has been escalated to the Strategic Risk Register at the request of the Senior Leadership Team. Not having an up-to-date local plan and non-compliance with national legislation [rated High Risk].

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Waste funding risk: Emissions Trading Scheme inclusion in 2028 may force changes to council waste budget allocation
findings.detail: The council has no agreement with Gloucestershire County Council to alter the payment mechanisms that incentivise recycling. However, the county could see waste budgets come under severe pressure in the coming years. Waste will enter the Emissions Trading Scheme in 2028, and this could force alterations to funding arrangements, creating financial risk.
findings.matters: A loss of recycling income or increase in recyclate processing costs would hit the council's budget without a clear offset mechanism, especially if ETS costs are passed through.
findings.figures: Waste enters Emissions Trading Scheme 2028
findings.quote: Whilst there remains no appetite from GCC to alter the payment mechanisms between them and SDC; in place to incentivise SDC to recycle more, the county could see waste budgets come under severe pressure in the coming years. Waste will become in scope of the Emissions Trading Scheme in 2028 (recorded as a service risk) and this pressure has the potential for alterations to funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Net Zero investment gap: current funding constraints mean insufficient investment to meet 2030 Scope 1 and Scope 2 targets
findings.detail: The council faces a funding gap to deliver its Net Zero targets. Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions reductions are to be achieved by 2030, and Scope 3 by 2050. Given current funding constraints, the council acknowledges it is likely there will not be enough funding to invest in achieving these targets and associated adaptation and nature targets.
findings.matters: A funding shortfall on Net Zero creates exposure to future regulatory requirements and may require unplanned capital expenditure if government tightens environmental compliance rules.
findings.figures: Targets: Net Zero (Scope 1+2) by 2030; Scope 3 by 2050
findings.quote: Given current funding constraints it is likely that there will not be enough funding to invest in achieving Net Zero or Adaptation & nature targets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Inflation running higher than forecast: Medium-Term Financial Plan will require updating
findings.detail: Inflation is currently running slightly higher than the forecast that underpinned the MTFP. This will require updates to the financial plan, potentially increasing pressure on budgets across all services.
findings.matters: Higher-than-forecast inflation erodes purchasing power and increases the cost of delivering services, squeezing already tight budgets.
findings.figures: Inflation running higher than forecast (amount not specified)
findings.quote: Inflation is running slightly higher than forecast and this will be taken into account for the next update of the Medium-Term Financial Plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Budget settlement impact unknown until December 2025: government consultation scheduled for later in year
findings.detail: The council cannot quantify the direct financial impact on the general fund budget until the provisional settlement is announced in December 2025. Government consultation on local government funding is due later in the year. This timing delays the council's ability to finalise the Medium-Term Financial Plan and commit to spending decisions.
findings.matters: A council cannot lock in savings plans or service cuts until it knows the settlement, meaning a significant portion of the financial year will be run with provisional budgets.
findings.figures: Provisional settlement expected December 2025
findings.quote: Government consultation is due later in the year and the risk assessment will be updated at that point. The direct financial impact on SDC may not be known until the provisional settlement in December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: HRA facing multiple new cost pressures: Awaab's law, electrical safety testing, potential rent convergence, right to buy changes
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account faces convergence of new financial pressures. Electrical safety testing requirements come into force November 2025 and May 2026. Awaab's law compliance begins 27 October 2025. Rent convergence is under Government consultation (closing mid-August), and new right to buy rules plus minimum energy efficiency standards will add financial challenge. The council's 10-year rent settlement of CPI+1% provides some income certainty but the cumulative impact of these changes creates material financial risk.
findings.matters: These regulatory and legislative changes hit the HRA budget simultaneously, potentially squeezing the tenant-funded service and requiring either higher rents, lower spending, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Electrical safety testing: Nov 2025 and May 2026; Awaab's law: 27 Oct 2025; CPI+1% rent settlement extended to 10 years
findings.quote: Additional changes to electrical safety testing come in from Nov 25 and May 26 which will add pressure on the service, as well the commencement of Awaab's law from 27 Oct 2025. Other changes to right to buy and consultation on minimum energy efficiency standards and a new decent homes will also add financial challenge to the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Housing regulator compliance at risk: stock condition surveys below target, inspection possible within 2.5 years
findings.detail: The council faces potential regulatory intervention on Social Housing Regulation Act compliance. Stock condition surveys (required every 5 years) are lower than hoped. New legal requirements for Awaab's law and electrical safety compliance from October 2025 add pressure. The Housing Oversight Board has strengthened its approach and the council has scheduled its annual meeting with the regulator for 22 September; an inspection could happen at any stage during the next 2.5 years.
findings.matters: A housing regulator inspection or intervention would disrupt service delivery and potentially constrain the council's ability to develop new housing stock or maintain the existing estate.
findings.figures: Stock condition surveys below target; inspection window 2.5 years from June 2025
findings.quote: The self-assessment has identified some areas of weakness, but these are being addressed through improvement plans. For example we are aware our stock condition surveys (which should be carried out every 5 years) are not as high as we hoped. The additional legislative requirements for Awaab's law and changes to electrical safety will add additional pressure on the authority to comply with the safety and quality standard. An inspection could happen at any stage during the next 2.5 years.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Audit Completion Report - 2024_25
findings.headline: Fixed asset valuations have not been formally challenged or documented for at least two audit years
findings.detail: The council uses external valuers for land, buildings and council dwellings. While internal staff perform a sense check, the auditor states explicitly: 'The Council has not provided any evidence of challenge' to the valuer's assumptions. This finding has persisted from 2023/24 through 2024/25 with no documented action taken.
findings.matters: Fixed assets and council dwellings represent material balance sheet values; formal documented challenge to valuation assumptions ensures they reflect local market knowledge and council-specific circumstances rather than adopting external valuations unchallenged
findings.figures: Fixed asset valuations material to balance sheet but specific amounts not disclosed in this section
findings.quote: The Council has not provided any evidence of challenge but confirmed that this was part of internal discussions with the internal valuation team.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Audit Completion Report - 2024_25
findings.headline: Pension liability assumptions have not been formally reviewed and documented for three audit years
findings.detail: The external actuary (Hymans Robertson LLP) sets assumptions on CPI, RPI and discount rates affecting pension liability valuation. Management performs only an informal 'sense check' without documentation. Despite flagging since 2022/23, management stated in 2024/25 that it 'considers that there is limited review that they can undertake' and has not implemented a documented review process.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a material deferred obligation; documented challenge to actuarial assumptions demonstrates governance and ensures assumptions align with the council's internal expectations rather than simply accepting the actuary's proposals
findings.figures: Pension liabilities material but specific amounts not disclosed in this section
findings.quote: Management have not changed their consideration of this recommendation, where there should be some consideration of the overall assumptions used by the valuer (e.g. salary increase estimate) compared to the internal expectations of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 10 - Stroud District Council - Audit Completion Report - 2024_25
findings.headline: Staff cost reconciliation between payroll and general ledger is not being performed
findings.detail: Audit testing identified that the council is not performing a monthly reconciliation between payroll records and the general ledger. The auditor recommended establishing this control; management's response is awaited. This is a current-year control deficiency.
findings.matters: Staff costs are typically a material expense; the absence of reconciliation creates risk of undetected posting errors, duplicate payments, or expense misstatement
findings.figures: No specific amount; relates to overall staff cost posting accuracy
findings.quote: From our testing of staff costs, reconciling the payroll records to the general ledger and financial statements, we identified that a reconciliation was not being performed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Recommendation Moitoring – Recommendations Exceeded Implementation Date
findings.headline: High-priority leasehold service charge control weaknesses remain unresolved 20+ months after original recommendation dates.
findings.detail: Three high-rated audit recommendations concerning Section 20 leaseholder service charges all exceeded their target implementation dates (original: March–April 2024, revised to July 2025). The recommendations required documented oversight checks, reconciliation procedures, risk registration, and process documentation. Although marked 'completed' in June 2025, the October 2025 update states: 'Evidence will be compiled and provided before next ASC', indicating the controls are not yet operational or verified.
findings.matters: Service charge collection is direct council income; unresolved control weaknesses here indicate gaps in financial management and the council's ability to implement internal controls effectively.
findings.figures: Recommendations dated 31/03/2025 (revised 31/07/2025), 30/04/2024, and 31/12/2024; July 2025 marked as 'completed'; October 2025 update: evidence compilation still pending.
findings.quote: Update October 2025 - Evidence will be compiled and provided before next ASC.

findings.paper_title: Half Year Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital losses of £311k realised from terminated property funds reduce reserves
findings.detail: Lothbury Property Fund and Hermes Property Fund both terminated during the first half of 2025-26, crystallising capital losses of £120k and £191k respectively. The council's original £10m investment in property and multi-asset funds has been revalued to £5.45m. These losses will be fully funded from the Investment Risk Earmarked Reserve which stands at £586k, with no impact on the General Fund outturn for 2025-26.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track reserve drawdowns and exposure to market risks. Reserves declining from anticipated losses—even if managed through earmarked provisions—signals a finite buffer and reflects property market exposure that has materialised.
findings.figures: £10m originally invested, revalued at £5.45m as at 30 September 2025; capital losses of £311k (Lothbury £120k, Hermes £191k); Investment Risk Earmarked Reserve £586k
findings.quote: The Council originally invested £10m into Property and Multi-Asset Funds, and as at 30 September 2025 it is revalued at £5.45m following redemptions from the Lothbury and Hermes Property Funds.
